title: Wick Play
teaches: The wick play as we trade it: a strong leader closes off its high and leaves an upper wick, the next day holds inside that wick and above the body, the buy is a market order as price breaks the prior day's high, the stop sits a few cents under the prior day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

questions.q: In one line, what is a wick play?
choices: A hold in the prior day's upper wick
A buy off a long lower wick at support
A gap up out of a long flat base
A reversal after a sweep of the low
questions.answer: A hold in the prior day's upper wick
questions.why: A hold in the prior day's upper wick. First a strong stock closes off its high and leaves an upper wick. The next day opens in that wick and holds there, without trading in the body. TaPlot calls that hold a sign of strength. It is not a bounce off a lower wick.
questions.lesson_line: A wick play is a hold inside yesterday's upper wick.

wrong.A buy off a long lower wick at support: A wick play holds in the prior day's upper wick, above the body. A lower wick at support is a different idea.
wrong.A reversal after a sweep of the low: That is a Go Signal. It sweeps support and leaves a lower wick. A wick play holds in the upper wick.
wrong.A gap up out of a long flat base: The next day opens below the prior high, inside the wick, not above it. Then it holds in that wick.

questions.simple: It is a day that stays inside yesterday's upper wick without dipping into the body, which is a sign of strength.

reasons: the upper-wick reading rests on the card default while D-010 (lower wick in the house glossary) and D-116 (wick size) are pending

questions.q: Our card reads a long upper wick, on its own, as bearish.
questions.why: True. Our card: read alone, a long upper wick is bearish. The setup only flips that when the hold works. The next day must hold inside the wick and not trade in the body. TaPlot calls that hold a sign of strength.
questions.lesson_line: A wick is a warning until the hold works.
questions.simple: True, because our card reads a long upper wick alone as bearish, until the next day holds inside it.

questions.q: Day 1 is red: it opened 48.20 and closed 47.65. Where is the body top?
choices: 48.20, the open
47.65, the close
The body's midpoint
The day's high
questions.why: 48.20, the open. The body top is the larger of the open and the close, the line Deepvue's test uses. On a red day the open is the larger, so it is the top. The close, 47.65, is the bottom of the body. The upper wick runs from the body top up to the high.
questions.lesson_line: The body top is the larger of the open and the close.

wrong.The day's high: The high is the top of the wick. The body top is the larger of the open and the close.
wrong.47.65, the close: The close is the lower end of a red body. The body top is the larger of the two.
wrong.The body's midpoint: The midpoint sits inside the body. The top is the larger of the open and the close.

questions.simple: The body top is 48.20, the open, because on a red day the open is higher than the close.

questions.q: Buying the wick day itself is the setup.
questions.why: False. The wick day is only day 1. The signal is the next day's hold inside that wick. Buying day 1 itself is a named mistake on our card. We wait for the hold, then buy the break of the prior day's high.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy the wick. Wait for the hold.
questions.simple: False, because the wick day only sets up the trade and the next day's hold is the real signal.

reasons: trigger timing (strict day 3 or same-day push) is pending D-115; the key holds under both

questions.q: What is the trigger on a wick play?
choices: A break of the prior day's high
The wick day's own close
A later dip to the 21 EMA
A close over the prior high
questions.answer: A break of the prior day's high
questions.why: A break of the prior day's high. Our card names the trigger the prior day's high break. TaPlot: the trigger is price moving over the high of the wick inside day. The move over the high is the trigger, not a close above it. It is not the wick day's close either. Buying day 1 skips the hold, and the hold is the signal.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is a break of the prior day's high.

wrong.The wick day's own close: Buying day 1 itself skips the hold. The hold is the signal.
wrong.A later dip to the 21 EMA: That is Manrav's pullback-to-the-21-EMA entry. Our card lists it as not ours.
wrong.A close over the prior high: The trigger is price moving over the prior day's high. It does not wait for a close.

questions.simple: The trigger is price breaking over the prior day's high, not a close above it.

reasons: the trigger rests on the strict versus same-day form held in D-115 (the key holds under every option)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We enter a wick play with a ___ order.
questions.why: market. Entries are market orders. On a wick play the order goes in when price crosses the trigger. The trigger is the break of the prior day's high, in regular trading hours. A limit, stop-limit or limit-on-close order is not our entry.
questions.lesson_line: Entries are market orders in regular hours.
questions.simple: Market, because we buy at market the moment price crosses the trigger.

reasons: house rule from the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: On a day-3 buy, the stop sits a few cents under day 2's low.
questions.why: True. On a day-3 buy, the stop sits a few cents under day 2's low. That is the prior day's low at the time of the buy. It goes a few cents under, not exactly on it. Set the stop first and size from it. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip. Moving it under day 1's low for room is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under day 2's low.
questions.simple: True, the stop goes a few cents under day 2's low, which is the prior day's low when you buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62) and the day-3 form held in D-115

questions.why: An Oops. It opened at 49.60, under the prior close of 50.00. It fell to 48.90, under the prior low of 49.20, then closed back over it. That is the Oops shape. A wick play's day 2 opens above the prior day's body top.
questions.lesson_line: Under the low and back is an Oops. A hold above the body is a wick play.

wrong.A wick play on day 2: A wick play's day 2 opens above the prior body top and holds there. This opened at 49.60, under the prior close.
wrong.An inside day in range: An inside day stays inside the prior day's range. This one fell to 48.90, under the low of 49.20.
wrong.A Kicker gap setup: A Kicker gaps over the prior close. This day opened under it, at 49.60.

questions.story: Yesterday closed at 50.00, with a low of 49.20. Today opened at 49.60 and fell to 48.90. Then it closed back at 50.40.
questions.simple: An Oops, because it opened under yesterday's close and dipped below yesterday's low before taking it back.

deeper.counter: A wick play starts from strength. Day 1 is a strong bar with a wick above, and day 2 opens inside that wick. An Oops opens under the prior close and dips under the prior low. The open alone tells them apart.

reasons: criterion wk.day2_same_day is pending D-115; the key holds under every option

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Go Signal
A wick play
An Oops
A Kicker
questions.why: A Go Signal. Its day opens under the prior close, sweeps support and leaves a lower wick as buyers step in. A wick play is a different picture. Its day 2 opens above the prior body top, in the upper wick, and holds there without trading in the body.
questions.lesson_line: Lower wick after a sweep is not a wick play.

wrong.A wick play: A wick play holds in the prior day's upper wick. This day opened under the prior close and left a lower wick.
wrong.A Kicker: This day opened under yesterday's close. It did not gap up over yesterday's high.
wrong.An Oops: This day held above yesterday's low and never traded under it.

questions.story: Today opened under yesterday's close and swept below a support level. It held above yesterday's low. Buyers stepped in and left a long lower wick.
questions.simple: A Go Signal, because it swept support and left a lower wick, while a wick play holds in the upper wick.

deeper.trap: Both setups show a long wick and buyers stepping in, so they are easy to mix up. Look at which wick and where the day opens. A Go Signal opens under the prior close and leaves a lower wick. A wick play's day 2 opens above the prior body top, up in the upper wick.

reasons: rests on the card's upper-wick default held in D-010
fixed before

questions.q: Is this a wick play?
choices: No, its low dipped into the body
Yes, it stayed under day 1's high
Yes, a 57% wick is long enough
No, it never broke day 1's high
questions.answer: No, its low dipped into the body
questions.why: No. Day 2's low of 163.35 dips under day 1's body top of 165.51, so it traded into the body. Our card calls that an inside day that touched the body, not a wick play. Staying under day 1's high is only half the test.
questions.lesson_line: A real dip into the body ends the wick play.

wrong.Yes, it stayed under day 1's high: Staying under the high is half of it. The low also has to stay above the body top.
wrong.No, it never broke day 1's high: Staying under day 1's high is part of the pattern, not a fail. The fail here is the dip into the body.
wrong.Yes, a 57% wick is long enough: The wick's size is not the fail here. Day 2's low traded into the body, and that ends it.

questions.story: Day 1 has a 57% upper wick and a body top of 165.51. Day 2 stays under day 1's high but its low is 163.35.
questions.simple: No, because day 2's low of 163.35 fell below the body top at 165.51, and a wick play must stay above it.

deeper.trap: Measure the dip, do not eyeball it. Here the low was 1.3% under the body top, 0.54 ATR. The tolerance for a dip is still open. This one is a real dip, and our card files it as a near-miss, not a wick play.

reasons: the body-touch tolerance is pending D-116 and criterion wk.day2_strict D-115; the key holds under every option

questions.q: Valid or void?
choices: Void; it traded into the body
Valid; it closed back in the wick
Valid; the open was in the wick
Void; it opened above day 1's close
questions.answer: Void; it traded into the body
questions.why: Void. Day 1 opened at 40.00 and closed at 42.00, so its body runs from 40.00 up to 42.00. Day 2 sold off to 40.30, near the bottom of the body. Our card treats day 2 trading well into the body as a no-trade. The close back in the wick does not undo it. TaPlot's sign of strength is holding in the wick without trading in the body.
questions.lesson_line: A close back in the wick does not undo a drop into the body.

wrong.Valid; the open was in the wick: The open was fine. The sell-off into the body is what failed.
wrong.Valid; it closed back in the wick: Where day 2 closes is not the test. The drop to 40.30, well into the body, voids it.
wrong.Void; it opened above day 1's close: Opening above the body top, in the wick, is what a wick play's day 2 does. The fault is the drop to 40.30.

questions.story: Day 1 opened 40.00, ran to 46.00 and closed at 42.00. Day 2 opened at 44.50, sold off to 40.30, and closed at 45.20. Its high was 45.80.
questions.simple: Void, because day 2 dropped well into day 1's body, and a close back in the wick does not fix that.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging by the close. Day 2 ended back in the wick, so it looks like the hold worked. But the drop to 40.30 had already broken it. A wick play is about where day 2 trades all day, not where it ends up.

reasons: the body-touch tolerance is held in D-116 (a drop to 40.30, 1.70 under the 42.00 body top, is well into the body under every option)

questions.q: By Deepvue's test, which day 2 is a wick play?
choices: Low 12.40 and high 12.80
questions.why: Low 12.40 and high 12.80. Deepvue's test: day 2's low is above the larger of day 1's open or close. Its high is below day 1's high. That puts it above the body top of 12.30 and under the high of 13.00. The whole day sits inside the wick.
questions.lesson_line: Above the body top, under the high.

wrong.Low 12.10, high 12.70: The low of 12.10 is under the body top of 12.30. It traded into the body.
wrong.Low 12.50, high 13.20: The high of 13.20 is over day 1's high of 13.00. Deepvue's test wants the high below it.
wrong.Low 11.80, high 12.20: The whole day sits under the body top of 12.30, not in the wick. A wick play's day 2 sits above it.

questions.story: Day 1 has a high of 13.00 and a body top of 12.30. Four candidates for day 2 follow.
questions.simple: Low 12.40 and high 12.80, because it is the only day 2 that stays above the body top and under day 1's high.

deeper.counter: An ordinary inside day may sit anywhere inside day 1's range. Low 11.80, high 12.20 may be one, yet it sits under the body top. Only a day 2 above the body top and under the high passes Deepvue's test.

reasons: the strict versus same-day form is held in D-115 (the question now names Deepvue's strict test)

questions.q: Which setup grades higher?
choices: A, stronger on each of the cues
B, its wider stop gives room
The same, as both are leaders
B, a Yellow market is calmer
questions.answer: A, stronger on each of the cues
questions.why: A. Every cue on our card points to A. It is a true leader, RS 90 or more in the strongest group. Its stop is within 3%, and the market is Green. B passes our leader rule but is under RS 90. Its stop is wider than 3%, which cuts the size, and the market is Yellow.
questions.lesson_line: Leader, tight stop and Green tend to grade higher.

wrong.B, its wider stop gives room: A wider stop only means a smaller size, and B's market is weaker too.
wrong.The same, as both are leaders: Both pass our leader rule, but the cues still differ. A is the true leader, with the tighter stop and the Green market.
wrong.B, a Yellow market is calmer: Our card lists Green as the stronger cue and Yellow as the weaker one.

questions.story: Setup A: RS 93 in the strongest group, a 1.4% stop, a Green market. Setup B: RS 85 in a strong group, a 4.1% stop, a Yellow market.
questions.simple: A, because it has the stronger stock, the tighter stop and the better market, while B is weaker on all three.

deeper.counter: A wider stop is not extra upside. For the same dollar risk, B's 4.1% stop buys far fewer shares than A's 1.4% stop. The card cuts B's size to fit. Room to run is not what a wider stop buys.

reasons: fixed before (silly choice and grade labels, 2026-11-10)

questions.q: Was the trade a mistake?
choices: No, a planned loss; the run ended
Yes, the stop was too tight
Yes, you should have held on
No, but the rule failed
questions.answer: No, a planned loss; the run ended
questions.why: No. The stop did its job. You bought at 101.33 with a 1.1% stop, and the next session's low of 99.49 took it. A perfect-looking wick play at the end of a run is still a 1%-stop bet on one more push. The rule did not fail. The run was over.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out under the rules is a planned loss.

wrong.Yes, the stop was too tight: The stop is the exit, and it did its job. In the next 20 sessions the stock never traded above 102.53.
wrong.Yes, you should have held on: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.No, but the rule failed: The rule did not fail. The run was over, and the stop took a planned loss.

questions.story: You buy at 101.33 with a 1.1% stop. The next session's low is 99.49 and you are stopped out. In the next 20 sessions it never trades above 102.53.
questions.simple: No, the stop did its job, because a stop-out under the rules is a planned loss, not a mistake.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging a trade by its result. AMZN in 2018 looked perfect: a 60% wick, a clean inside day, a fill 1.1% under the 52-week high. It was stopped the next session. The stop is the exit, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21)

questions.q: Which cue was missing?
choices: A fresh explosion before day 1
A bigger upper wick on day 1
A much tighter stop on the buy
A stop under day 1's low instead
questions.why: A fresh explosion. The card's review found no explosion in the prior 15 sessions. It was a wick play in a pullback, not after a burst, with a stop inside the noise. A fresh explosion is a grading plus, not a requirement, so this was a weaker case, not a broken rule.
questions.lesson_line: An explosion first, then the hold, is the stronger case.

wrong.A bigger upper wick on day 1: The wick was already 91% of day 1's range. Its size was not what was missing.
wrong.A much tighter stop on the buy: The 0.75% stop was already tight. The review says it sat inside the noise, the opposite problem.
wrong.A stop under day 1's low instead: Moving the stop under day 1's low to give it room is a named mistake on our card.

questions.story: Day 1 had a 91% wick and day 2 sat wholly inside it. You bought at 178.42 with a 0.75% stop. The next session took the stop. In the prior 15 sessions the stock had no big gap or volume burst.
questions.simple: A fresh explosion, because the stock had no big gap or volume burst first, so it was a weaker pullback case.

deeper.trap: Do not read one loss as a new rule. The missing explosion made this a weaker case, but a fresh explosion is a plus, not a must. The lesson is to grade such a pullback lower, not to refuse every wick play without a burst.

reasons: fixed before (grade labels, 2026-11-10)

questions.q: The stop fills on the entry day. What now?
choices: Take the loss; rebuy on a new setup
Buy back at once to catch the run
Lower the stop on the next try for room
Skip the stop order on the next try
questions.answer: Take the loss; rebuy on a new setup
questions.why: Take the loss. A stop is a stop, even when the stock later climbs to 4.5R without you. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again. That is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Its stop still goes a few cents under the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped is stopped, even if it runs later.

wrong.Skip the stop order on the next try: Every position has a real stop order with the broker. A stop that hurt once is still the exit.
wrong.Buy back at once to catch the run: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again.
wrong.Lower the stop on the next try for room: The next stop still goes a few cents under the prior day's low. Lowering it for room is no fix.

questions.story: You buy over day 2's high. The stock reverses the same day and takes your stop. Over the next 20 sessions it climbs to 4.5R without you.
questions.simple: Take the loss, because a stop is a stop, and you buy again only if the setup triggers again.

deeper.trap: ANET in our research did exactly this. It was stopped on the entry day on any ordering of the bars, then reached 4.5R within 20 sessions. Hindsight says the stop was wrong. The rule says a stop is a stop. Buying back at once breaks the rebuy rule.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B21, E56)

questions.q: Which rule should have kept you out?
choices: No new buys 3 days before a report
Never buy more than 4% over the trigger
Put the stop under day 1's low
questions.answer: No new buys 3 days before a report
questions.why: No new buys 3 days before a report. The fill at 91.40 had a 2.75% stop, and the next open at 77.80 was 15% lower on the earnings reaction.
questions.lesson_line: A clean pattern still gaps on earnings.

wrong.Never buy more than 4% over the trigger: The fill was at the trigger. The chase rule was not the issue.
wrong.Put the stop under day 1's low: A wider stop only makes a gap loss bigger.

questions.story: A strict wick play prints. You buy at 91.40 with a 2.75% stop. The next day it opens at 77.80, 15% lower, through the stop.

questions.q: Does the earnings rule block the buy today?
choices: No, nine days out is clear
Yes, nine days is too close
Yes, but only at half size
No, a strong RS lifts the rule
questions.answer: No, nine days out is clear
questions.why: No. The no-buy window is the 3 days before a report. Nine days out is clear, so the earnings rule does not stop this buy. Watch the date as the trade runs: holding through the report is only for a trade up 5R by then.
questions.lesson_line: Only the 3 days before a report are off limits.

wrong.Yes, but only at half size: Half size is not part of the rule. The window is the 3 days before a report.
wrong.No, a strong RS lifts the rule: The answer is no, but not for that reason. The rule has no RS exception. Nine days out is simply outside the 3-day window.
wrong.Yes, nine days is too close: The window is the 3 days before a report. Nine days out is outside it.

questions.story: A clean wick play with RS 92 in the strongest group. The report is nine days away.
questions.simple: No, because only the 3 days before a report are off limits, and this report is nine days away.

deeper.trap: Clear for the buy is not clear for the hold. Nine days later the report arrives. Unless the trade is up 5R by then, our rule says do not hold through it. Know the report date when you buy.

reasons: one cited fact only
house rule from the owner's rulebook (B22)
the window changed (owner set it to 3 days)
fixed before (B22 only, 2026-11-10)

questions.q: By Deepvue's definition, the whole of day 2 sits inside day 1's upper wick.
questions.why: True. Deepvue: the low of the current candle is greater than the larger of the prior day's open or close. Its high is less than the prior day's high. So the whole day sits in the prior upper wick. An ordinary inside day may sit anywhere inside day 1's range.
questions.lesson_line: Deepvue's test: day 2 inside day 1's wick.
questions.simple: True, because Deepvue puts day 2's low above day 1's body top and its high below day 1's high.

deeper.counter: Deepvue's test leaves no room for a dip into the body. Day 2's low must be above the larger of day 1's open and close. An ordinary inside day may sit anywhere inside day 1's range, so not every inside day is a wick play.

questions.q: Take it?
choices: Take it: market order on the break
Wait for the close, then buy
Pass; the report is too close
Pass; 4% over the 10-day is stretched
questions.answer: Take it: market order on the break
questions.why: Take it. Every check here passes. RS 90 in a leading group makes it a leader. It sits above the 50-day and 200-day, with the 50 over the 200. At 4% over the 10-day it is under our 10% stretch line. Day 2 held inside the wick, the market is Green and the report is three weeks out. The buy is a market order as price crosses the trigger. The stop sits a few cents under day 2's low.
questions.lesson_line: All gates pass: market order on the break, stop under the low.

wrong.Wait for the close, then buy: The trigger is the break of the prior day's high, and the order is a market order when price crosses it. A close is not the trigger.
wrong.Pass; the report is too close: The window is the 3 days before a report. Three weeks out is clear.
wrong.Pass; 4% over the 10-day is stretched: Our stretch line is 10% over the 10-day average. At 4% it is not stretched.

questions.story: A stock with RS 90, in a leading group, sits above its 50-day and 200-day, with the 50 over the 200. It is 4% over its 10-day, and day 2 held inside day 1's wick. The market is Green and the report is three weeks away. Price trades over day 2's high.
questions.simple: Take it, because every check here passes, so you buy at market as price breaks day 2's high.

deeper.trap: Do not add a step the plan does not have. Waiting for a close sounds careful, but the trigger is price crossing day 2's high, and the market order goes in there. Each check in this story was a before-the-buy check, and all of them passed.

reasons: house rules from the owner's rulebook (B22, C29, C31, E57, F65); trigger timing pending D-115
fixed before (10-day distance added 2026-11-10)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before the break. On the pattern alone, take it or pass?
choices: Take it; it holds inside the wick
Pass; the last bar dipped into the body
Pass; the wick is too small
Take it now, at today's close
questions.answer: Take it; it holds inside the wick
questions.why: Take it. Day 1 closed off its high with a 70% upper wick. Day 2 sat wholly inside that wick, its low of 189.04 above the body top of 188.62. The buy is the break over day 2's high the next session, at market, not a buy at day 2's close.
questions.lesson_line: Last bar inside the wick, above the body: take the break.

wrong.Pass; the last bar dipped into the body: Look again: the low of the last bar stays above the body top of the bar before it.
wrong.Pass; the wick is too small: The upper wick is most of the first bar's range.
wrong.Take it now, at today's close: The trigger is a break of the prior day's high. Buying the close of day 2 is early: the break has not printed.

questions.simple: Take it, because the last bar holds inside the upper wick above the body, so you buy the break of its high.

deeper.example: This was MELI, February 2017. Day 2 ranged 190.70 to 189.04 on 0.44x volume. The buy came at 190.71, a cent over day 2's high, with the stop at 189.01. 3R printed on day 5 and 5R on day 7.

reasons: criterion wk.day2_strict pending D-115; the strict day-3 buy is the dossier's example
fixed before (2026-11-10)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before the break. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; it closed under the 200-day
Take it; the upper wick is long
Take it; day 2 is inside the wick
Pass; the close is under the 50-day
questions.why: Pass. The close sat 2.2% under the 200-day, and we take no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long. The card's trend check also wants the 50-day over the 200-day. Here the 50-day sat 10.2% under it. The two-day shape does not override the averages.
questions.lesson_line: Check the averages before the candles.

wrong.Take it; day 2 is inside the wick: The two-day shape is fine. The close is under the 200-day, so there is no long.
wrong.Pass; the close is under the 50-day: The close sat above the 50-day. The 50-day was 10.2% under the 200-day and the close only 2.2% under it. The fail is the 200-day.
wrong.Take it; the upper wick is long: A long wick is only the first bar. The close under the 200-day fails first.

questions.simple: Pass, because the stock closed under its 200-day, and we take no longs below the 200-day.

deeper.trap: A neat two-day pattern pulls the eye. Check the averages first: the close over the 200-day and the 50-day. Here the close was 2.2% under the 200-day, so the shape never gets a vote.

reasons: house 200-day rule from the owner's rulebook (B26)
fixed before (day-2 averages, 2026-11-10)

questions.q: Do you buy?
choices: No, not outside regular hours
Yes, the trigger came early
Yes, if you use limit orders
No, it resets the trigger
questions.why: No. We make no new buys outside regular trading hours, and 8:15 in premarket is outside them. Entries are market orders, placed in the regular session. The trigger stays day 2's high, and the buy waits for the regular session.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for regular hours.

wrong.Yes, the trigger came early: Price over the trigger in premarket is not a buy. No new buys outside regular hours.
wrong.Yes, if you use limit orders: A limit order is still a new buy outside regular hours, and our entries are market orders.
wrong.No, it resets the trigger: The trigger stays the prior day's high. The rule only stops a new buy outside regular hours.

questions.story: On day 3, price trades over day 2's high at 8:15 in the morning, in premarket.
questions.simple: No, because we never start a new buy before the regular session opens, even if price is already over the trigger.

reasons: house rules from the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Trail a fast mover under the ___-day average.
questions.why: 10. Trail a fast mover under the 10-day average and a steadier one under the 21-day. Sell on a close below it, not on a dip under it during the day. The trail carries the last third, after the trims at 3R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Fast mover, 10-day. Steadier, 21-day.
questions.simple: 10, because a fast mover trails under its 10-day average and you sell on a close below it.

reasons: house trail rule from the owner's rulebook (E51, E52)

questions.q: Is this a wick play?
choices: Yes, day 2 sits inside the wick
No, a red day cannot set it up
No, day 2 is under the open
Yes, it broke day 1's high
questions.answer: Yes, day 2 sits inside the wick
questions.why: Yes. Day 1 is red, so its body top is the open, 32.46. Day 2's low of 32.57 is above it. Its high of 33.36 is under day 1's high of 34.00. The whole day sits inside the wick. The close, 32.11, is the bottom of a red body, not the test line.
questions.lesson_line: Red day: the body top is the open.

wrong.No, a red day cannot set it up: A red day can set it up. Deepvue's test uses the larger of the open and close, so a red day's top is its open.
wrong.No, day 2 is under the open: The open is 32.46. Day 2's low of 32.57 is above it.
wrong.Yes, it broke day 1's high: Day 2's high of 33.36 is under day 1's 34.00, so it did not break it. It stayed inside the wick.

questions.story: Day 1 is red: open 32.46, high 34.00, close 32.11. Day 2 trades between 32.57 and 33.36.
questions.simple: Yes, because day 2 stays above the red day's open of 32.46 and under its high of 34.00.

questions.q: What can the stop do now?
choices: Move up to breakeven
Move down to give it room
Widen it to the 21-day
Nothing, stops are fixed
questions.why: Move up to breakeven. Our rule moves the stop to breakeven between 2R and 5R, ideally. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Past 3R, with a third banked, breakeven is in range. It never goes lower to give the rest room.
questions.lesson_line: After the first trim, breakeven is allowed. Never lower.

wrong.Move down to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Widen it to the 21-day: That is wider. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Nothing, stops are fixed: Stops are not frozen. They only move up, and breakeven between 2R and 5R is the rule.

questions.story: The first session closes past 3R and you take a third off. The rest still has the original stop under day 2's low.
questions.simple: Move it up to breakeven, because past 3R the stop may rise to your buy price, and it never goes down.

reasons: one source only (the rulebook)
rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B19)

questions.q: What becomes the stop?
choices: The first 30-minute low
The original stop at 48.50
The prior day's low
The gap-down open at 48.10
questions.why: The first 30-minute low. On a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar, here 47.40, is the new stop. The ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. The loss to 47.40 is less than twice the planned risk, so it stays under 2R. This gap rule is the one exception to a stop that only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap, the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.The original stop at 48.50: The gap went through it. The first 30 minutes decide the new stop.
wrong.The prior day's low: After a gap against the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.
wrong.The gap-down open at 48.10: Our gap rule names the low of the first 30-minute bar as the new stop, not the open.

questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with the stop at 48.50. The stock gaps down and opens at 48.10. The first 30-minute low is 47.40.
questions.simple: The first 30-minute low, because on a gap the first 30 minutes set the new stop while the loss stays under 2R.

deeper.trap: The trap is the 2R ceiling. The 30-minute low becomes the stop only while the loss stays inside 2R. Had the first 30 minutes taken the stock past 2R, the rule says get out, not wait. The gap rule is also the one exception to a stop that only moves up.

reasons: one source only (the rulebook)
rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, A4)
computed check: the loss at 47.40 against 2R

questions.q: Which backdrop grades higher?
choices: The earnings gap, then the wick
The slow drift, then the wick
They grade the same
The drift, since gaps tend to fill
questions.answer: The earnings gap, then the wick
questions.why: The earnings gap, then the wick. Our card counts a leading group with fresh explosions (gaps, volume) as a cue, and a recent explosion as a grading plus. Setup A is that frame: a 10% gap on 5x volume 14 sessions ago, then a wick day on the 10-day EMA. Setup B has no recent catalyst. B is weaker, not banned: the explosion is a plus, not a requirement.
questions.lesson_line: Explosion first, then the pause.

wrong.The slow drift, then the wick: A slow drift with no recent catalyst is the weaker backdrop.
wrong.They grade the same: A fresh explosion makes the stronger case and a slow drift the weaker one.
wrong.The drift, since gaps tend to fill: Our card counts a fresh gap on volume as a plus. Setup A's gap is the explosion the frame wants first.

questions.story: Setup A: a 10% earnings gap on 5x volume 14 sessions ago, then a wick day on the 10-day EMA. Setup B: a slow drift with no news for months, then a wick day.
questions.simple: The earnings gap setup, because a fresh burst on big volume before the wick makes the stronger case.

reasons: fixed before (grade labels, 2026-11-10)

questions.q: A recent explosion is required before a wick play can be taken.
questions.why: False. A recent explosion, a fresh gap or volume burst, is a grading plus, not a requirement. Our card lists a leading group with fresh explosions as a cue. Without one, a wick play can still be taken.
questions.lesson_line: An explosion helps the grade. It is not a gate.
questions.simple: False, because a recent explosion only helps the grade, and a wick play can still be taken without one.

reasons: one source only (the card)

questions.q: What do you do on day 3?
choices: Buy; 3.72% is inside the 4% limit
Skip; the open is past 4%

questions.why: 12,000. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 1,200,000 is 12,000. The risk math gives a size first, then the caps trim it, so the smallest number wins. The 40% cap does not bind here. One quiet day does not set the volume cap. The average does.

wrong.20,000 shares, over two days: The cap is on what you own, not on one day's buying. Never own more than 1% of the average daily volume.
